title: Where to eat
intro: A note on tourist-trap avoidance: the generic “best restaurants in Sedona” lists skew toward the Uptown strip closest to hotels — this guide deliberately routes through spots local guides actually name as where residents eat.

items.name: Wildcraft Cafe
items.hours: ⚠ Varies by day of week — confirm before you go
items.why: Health-conscious, organic, vegan/paleo/gluten-free options — an easy local breakfast or lunch that isn't a hotel buffet.

items.name: Elote Cafe
items.why: Sedona's most in-demand table — bold, elevated Southwestern and Mexican cooking.
items.crowd_tip: Reserve ahead, especially on a weekend — it's not a reliable walk-in.

items.name: El Rincon
items.why: Sedona's original Mexican restaurant (since 1976) — Arizona-style with Navajo/Hopi influence; the chimichanga (real sopapilla masa, fried, served enchilada-style) is the house specialty, and it sits right inside Tlaquepaque so it pairs naturally with that stop.

items.name: Tamaliza
items.why: Built around tamales specifically, not general Mexican — fresh-made daily with organic non-GMO masa, family recipes from Guerrero/Michoacán/Puebla/Oaxaca, vegan and vegetarian options included. A distinct specialty from El Rincon, not a second version of the same thing.
items.hours: ⚠ Closed Mondays; Tue–Sun 9am–4pm — confirm before you go

items.name: Coffee Pot Restaurant
items.why: A west-side local institution for 30+ years — a straightforward, unpretentious breakfast spot.

items.name: Judi's Restaurant & Lounge
items.why: A scratch-kitchen local institution since 1986 (same owners since 2013) — classic American with a warm, unhurried, slightly old-school dining-room feel rather than an Uptown tourist stop.
items.hours: ⚠ Closed Sundays; otherwise ≈11am–8:30pm — confirm before you go

items.name: The Golden Goose
items.why: West-side steak, seafood, and burger spot open from breakfast through dinner — a practical any-time option that isn't a Mexican restaurant, on a stretch locals actually use rather than the Uptown strip.

items.name: Butterfly Burger
items.why: Casual burgers and cocktails near the Village of Oak Creek, south of central Sedona — later hours than most picks here, useful if dinner plans slip.

items.name: The Hudson
items.why: Chef Jeff Storcz's elevated comfort food (burgers, fish, ribs, steak) in an industrial-chic room with one of the better views in town — a step up for a night that isn't the Elote splurge.

title: Shopping
intro: Tlaquepaque (see Sights) covers the courtyard-galleries side of Sedona shopping — these are genuinely different: a working trading post, a nonprofit arts-center gallery, a metaphysical/crystal specialist, a west-side crystal shop, and Gallery Row's small courtyard complex.

items.name: Garland's Navajo Rugs
items.why: A trading post built in traditional style, family-run since 1976 — one of the largest Navajo rug selections anywhere, plus Hopi kachina dolls, Pueblo pottery, sandpaintings, and handmade jewelry. A real specialist, not a souvenir-shop version of Native art.

items.name: Center for the New Age
items.why: Sedona's best-known metaphysical shop — one of the largest crystal and gemstone-jewelry selections in town, alongside psychic readings and healings if that's of interest. Leans into the vortex/New-Age side of Sedona rather than avoiding it.

items.name: Sedona Arts Center
items.why: A nonprofit gallery and working studio space (not a commercial gift shop) showing and selling local and regional artists' work, with classes and demonstrations running most weeks. A genuine arts-community stop rather than a retail one.

items.name: Hozho Distinctive Shops & Galleries
items.why: A small courtyard complex on Sedona's Gallery Row, Uptown — several independent galleries and boutiques under one roof, distinct from both Tlaquepaque's larger Spanish-colonial courtyards and the general Uptown strip. ⚠ Individual tenant galleries rotate — confirm which shops are currently open before making it the destination.

items.name: Crystal Magic
items.why: A straightforward west-side crystal, mineral, and gift shop — a lower-key alternative to Center for the New Age's readings-and-healings focus if you just want stones and gifts.
